title: The main line: 3.Nc3 and 4.d4
intro:
This is the line that has to be known best, because it is what most opponents play: the knight hits the queen, the pawn takes the centre, the other knight develops, and White has a normal position with an extra move. Black's answer is to put every piece on the square it wants and let White decide what to do with the move.

## The setup, and the one choice in it

After 3...Qd6 4.d4 Nf6 5.Nf3 the pawn goes to c6. That is the choice this chapter makes, and the other two are refused in a sentence each where they arise: 5...a6 is the other modern setup and has more to remember, and 5...Bg4 is right a move later and lets White take the bishop pair with a free move on the queen if it comes now.

With the pawn on c6 the queen has c7 to go to, the knights have no b5 or d5 to land on, and the light-squared bishop comes out to g4 or f5 before the pawn goes to e6. From there the position is a Caro-Kann and it is played like one.

## White's sixth moves

Five of them, and they are all about the light-squared bishop. 6.g3 takes the long diagonal and is the most testing; the answer is the pin on g4, and the bishop is chased to g6 and traded, which leaves Black solid with the h-file half open. 6.Ne5 tries to make the queen uncomfortable and costs White time doing it. 6.Bd3, 6.Bc4 and 6.h3 are the quiet ones. Against the two bishop moves Black pins on g4 and keeps the pin until White has paid for breaking it; 6.h3 has taken g4 away, so the bishop goes to f5 and is traded. Behind the bishop Black develops the same way against all three.

## What the queen does

It stays on d6 until it is asked to move, and then it goes to c7 or d8. It is not chased around for the sake of it: a queen move that answers a threat costs nothing, and a queen move made because the queen looks exposed is the tempo White was hoping for.

## Typical mistakes at this level

Moving the queen when nothing attacks it. Playing ...e6 before the bishop has come out. Recapturing on g6 with the f-pawn, which opens the king, when the h-pawn keeps the structure and gives the rook a file. Meeting Ne5 with ...Nbd7 and then forgetting that the knight on c4 hits the queen next. And taking on f3 with the bishop when it was not asked, which hands White the bishop pair for nothing.

tree.note: The most testing sixth move. The bishop is going to g2, where it looks down the long diagonal at the queenside Black is about to develop on.

children.note: The pin, and this is the moment for it. The bishop comes outside the pawns before e6, and it ties the knight to the queen.

mistakes.note: Also sound. Against the fianchetto the pin is the sharper choice, because the knight on f3 is what makes White's whole setup work.
The bishop is shut in behind its own pawn, which is the one thing this structure exists to avoid.
Two fianchettos facing each other leaves Black a tempo down in a symmetrical position, and the queen on d6 with fewer squares.

children.note: The bishop takes its diagonal.
Now the pawn goes, with the bishop already out. The dark-squared bishop has e7 and the king is two moves from safety.

mistakes.note: Fine and it transposes. The pawn first means the bishop on f8 can come out whatever White does next.
Nobody asked. 8.Bxf3 gives White the bishop pair and the bishop on f3 is a strong piece on the long diagonal.

children.note: White castles and gets ready to ask the bishop a question with h3 and g4.
Develop and prepare to castle. The bishop has one square in this structure and this is it.

mistakes.note: Also good. The bishop first keeps castling one move away.
A useful square for the bishop later, and a move spent on nothing while the bishop on f8 is still at home.

children.note: The question. White wants to know whether the bishop trades or retreats.
Keep the pin. Trading now would give White the bishop pair for nothing, and the bishop on h5 still ties the knight down.

mistakes.note: 10.Bxf3 and White has the two bishops and a strong one on the long diagonal, for a pawn move that cost nothing.
Sound, and it gives up the pin. The bishop on h5 keeps the knight tied to the queen for another move.

children.note: White pushes the bishop again, at the cost of the pawn cover in front of the king.
The bishop retreats to the one square that keeps it on the board and outside the pawns. White will trade it, and the trade costs White the pawns in front of the king.

mistakes.note: The pawn is defended by the other pawn: 11.hxg4 Bxg4 and Black has two pawns for the knight, with no attack to show for it.

children.note: The knight comes to e5 to trade off the bishop.
Develop with a hit. The knight offers to trade on e5, and it covers the squares the queen needs.

mistakes.note: The queen moves before it is asked to. The knight does the same job and develops a piece doing it.
12.Nxg6 hxg6 leaves the knight on b8 still at home with the h-file open beside the king. The knight first.

children.note: White takes the bishop, which was the point of the pawn pushes.
Take back with the h-pawn, towards the centre. The rook on h8 has the half-open file, and the pawns in front of the king stay whole for castling.

mistakes.note: It opens the diagonal to the king and leaves the pawn on e6 backward, for a rook file the rook does not want.

children.plan: Castle short, put the queen on c7 and the rooks on d8 and the h-file, and play for the pawn to c5 against d4. White's king has pawns on g4 and h3 in front of it and nothing to attack with.
children.name: The full main line, 6.g3 to 12...hxg6

tree.note: The knight jumps in and plans Nc4, hitting the queen. It costs White two knight moves to gain one tempo.

children.note: Develop with a hit on the knight. It has to decide now, and both its moves give Black something.

mistakes.note: 7.Nc4 hits the queen, and the queen coming to f3 next hits the bishop, so Black is answering threats rather than developing.
Sound, and it moves the queen before it has been asked to. The knight move develops and makes White decide.

children.note: The knight hits the queen, which was the idea.
The queen goes to the square the pawn on c6 gave it. From c7 it watches the knight and the e5 square and is in the way of nothing.

mistakes.note: 8.Be3 blocks with a developing move and the queen is asked to move again, so the check has cost a tempo rather than gained one.
8.a3 hits the queen again and after 8...Qxc4 9.Bxc4 White has won the queen for a knight and a bishop.

children.note: White develops the queen, eyeing f7 and the long diagonal, and connects with the knight on c4.
Hit the knight back. It has to move or be traded, and either way Black gains the move.

mistakes.note: 9.dxe5 Nxe5 10.Nxe5 Qxe5+ 11.Be2 and White has traded a pair of knights and gained time on the queen again.
It lets the knight sit on c4 for free, and White's pieces arrive first. Hitting it is the move that gains the tempo back.

children.note: White hits the queen once more, with a developing move.
Back to d8. It looks like a retreat and it is: the queen has done its work, and from d8 it defends everything and blocks nothing.

mistakes.note: 10.Bxc7 and the bishop has taken the queen, because the queen was still on c7 with the bishop on f4 pointing at it.
It blocks the bishop on c8 in and leaves the queen on the file the rook is coming to.

children.note: The knight trades itself rather than retreat. Going back to e5 instead leaves the d-pawn to the queen.
The queen takes back and comes out for the third time, and this time it arrives with a threat: b2 is hanging and so is d4. Black has given up one tempo and taken two back, and the position is level.

mistakes.note: Sound, and it doubles the b-pawns to open the a-file. The queen recapture hits two pawns at once and keeps the structure.
The bishop hits the queen, but the knight on b6 is still standing: 11.Nxa8 and after 11...Bxf3 12.Nc7+ Kd7 13.gxf3 White has a rook for a bishop.
It hits two pieces and loses to both: 11.dxe5 Qxb6 12.exf6 and the pawn on f6 is worth more than the pawn on b2.

children.plan: If White castles long to hold b2 and d4, play the pawn to g6 and the bishop to g7, and keep the e-pawn home: with the bishop on f4 and the h-pawn coming, the pawn on e6 is a target. Otherwise take on d4 and give the pawn back later for development.
children.name: 6.Ne5 and the knight to c4

tree.note: The bishop takes the diagonal towards h7 and White castles next.

children.note: The pin. The bishop comes out before e6, and it ties the knight to the queen while White's own queen is still at home.

mistakes.note: 7.Bxf5 and nothing takes back: the bishop on d3 was pointing at f5.
The bishop is shut in, which this structure exists to avoid.

children.note: The question, asked at once.
Keep the pin. Nothing has asked for the bishop pair yet.

mistakes.note: 8.Qxf3 gives White the bishop pair and an active queen, for a pawn move.

children.note: White castles.
The pawn goes with the bishop already out.

mistakes.note: Fine, and it transposes. The pawn first frees the bishop on f8.

children.note: The rook comes to the open file, looking at the pawn on e6 and preparing Ne4.
Develop. The bishop covers the squares near the king and Black castles next.

mistakes.note: Also fine. The bishop first keeps castling one move away.

children.note: The knight jumps in, hitting the queen and the knight on f6 at once.
Trade it off. The knight was the piece with the ideas, and after the trade the bishop on h5 has nothing to fear.

mistakes.note: 11.Nxf6+ Bxf6 12.c4 hits the queen and White has traded the knight and gained a move.
11.Nxf6+ Bxf6 12.Bxh7 and the h-pawn goes, because the bishop on d3 was pointing at it all along.

children.note: The bishop takes back and stands in the centre.
Castle. The pieces are out, the trade has taken the sting out of White's setup, and the game is level.
children.plan: Knight to d7, queen to c7, and the pawn to c5 against d4. The bishop on h5 comes back to g6 to trade the one on e4 if it wants to.
children.name: 6.Bd3 and the knight to e4

tree.note: The bishop takes aim at f7 and at the d5 square.

children.note: The pin, as against 6.Bd3. The bishop on c4 looks at f7, and f7 is safe for as long as the queen stays on d6, which is exactly how long Black means it to stay.

mistakes.note: Playable, and it gives White a target: 7.Ne5 followed by g4 and h4 chases the bishop and gains time on the kingside. On g4 the bishop is pinning something.
Shut in again. The bishop comes out first.
7.Ng5 hits f7 with the knight and the bishop together, and Black has to spend a move on it.

children.note: White defends d4 against the pin and prepares to castle long.
The knight to d7, covering e5 so that White's knight cannot use the square to break the pin.

mistakes.note: Also fine. The knight first, because Ne5 is the move that asks the bishop a question.
Sound and active, and after 8.O-O e6 9.Nxd5 cxd5 10.Bb5+ the structure has changed into something the course does not teach.
The queen moves before it is asked to, and 8.h3 Bh5 9.g4 Bg6 10.Ne5 has White a move ahead in the chase.

children.note: White asks the bishop.
Keep the pin. The bishop is not asked to give up the diagonal yet.

mistakes.note: It gives up the bishop pair for nothing. Take on f3 when it wins something, not when it is asked.
Back to the square the pin left, and 9.O-O e6 10.Nh4 asks it again: the knight takes it or chases it to g6 and takes it there, and White has the two bishops for nothing.

children.note: The queen comes to e2 and White is ready to castle long.
The pawn goes with the bishop out.

mistakes.note: Fine, and it gives up the pin before White has paid for it with g4.
Sound. The pawn first, so that the bishop on f8 has somewhere to go.

children.note: White castles long and the kings will be on opposite sides.
Develop and prepare to castle the other way. Both sides are developed and it is a race, and Black's queenside pawns are ready to run first.

mistakes.note: The race starts a move early. Sound, and the bishop first means the king can leave the centre before the pawns go.
Castling into the side White's pawns are not on. Sound, and the plan is the other way: the king short and the queenside pawns forward.

children.plan: Castle short, then push the b-pawn to b5 at the bishop and on to b4 at the knight, with the queen on c7 behind it. If White plays g4 and Ne5 at the bishop, take on e5 and the pawn on e5 is a target rather than a threat.
children.name: 6.Bc4 and castling on opposite sides

tree.note: White takes g4 away from the bishop before it gets there.

children.note: The other square, and it is a good one: the bishop is outside the pawns and offers a trade White would rather not make.

mistakes.note: Shut in. The pawn on h3 took one square away, not both.

children.note: White offers the trade of bishops.
Take. The trade leaves White's queen on d3 in front of the d-pawn and Black with the simpler position.

mistakes.note: Sound, and 8.Bxg6 hxg6 gives Black the same trade with the pawns rearranged. Taking first keeps the structure.

children.note: The queen takes back and stands on the d-file.
The pawn goes. There is no bishop to shut in any more.

mistakes.note: Fine. The pawn first frees the bishop on f8.

children.note: White castles.
Develop.
The knight goes to e5, where it blocks the queen's diagonal. That is what makes the bishop coming to f4 next a real move rather than a hanging piece.
Castle. The knight on e5 is not doing anything yet, and the king is safer than the queen.

mistakes.note: Sound, and the queen has not been asked to move yet. Castle first and move it when it is hit.
Fine, and 11.Bf4 then makes Black choose between trading on e5 and moving the queen. Castling keeps the choice for later.

children.note: Now White hits the queen with a developing move, and the queen cannot take because the knight on e5 is in the way.
Back to d8, where it defends everything and blocks nothing. The queen has done its work and the position is level.

mistakes.note: 12.Nxd5 and the queen has walked onto the knight's square.
12.a3 chases it again and the queen has spent three moves to arrive on the edge.

children.plan: Put the knight on d7 and the queen on c7 or a5, and play for the pawn to c5. With the light-squared bishops gone there is nothing for White to attack.
children.name: 6.h3 and the bishops traded
